title: Capstone
premise: One substantial system that exercises the whole programme, shipped publicly and defended aloud. This is the artifact the transcript is built around, and it is the only course whose output a hiring manager will actually open. Everything before it was practice with a rubric attached; this is the thing itself, with the same rubrics applied to work nobody set for you.
why_here: Last, and gated on seven courses rather than a chain of two, because the point is integration. A capstone attempted before evaluation, retrieval, agents, inference, speech, transformers and architecture is a project with an AI feature in it. Attempted after, it is a system whose every component you can defend.
laboratory: Whatever you choose, subject to one rule: it must be something a stranger can use without you present. Not a notebook, not a demo you drive. The programme's other courses all borrowed their laboratory from products that already existed; this one has to produce a new one, because reusing an existing product would let you skip the part where a system meets someone who was not expecting it.
sitting_rule: Every item is completable in one sitting. Nothing exceeds 180 minutes, and anything over 90 declares its own checkpoints. A 120-hour project is 45 sittings, and the granularity is deliberate — it is what makes an irregular schedule survivable.
honesty_note: No advanced standing, and none is conceivable. The four existing products were built before this programme and cannot be resubmitted; the capstone must be new work, and the scope document registers what existed beforehand so the boundary is checkable.

panel.blind_note: Judges see the submission and the rubric, never each other's scores, and never the learner's self-assessment.
panel.disagreement: Scores are reported per judge and never averaged into a single number when the spread is 2 or more on any criterion.
panel.bias_warning: Judges are instructed to assess the system against its own registered scope rather than against an ideal one, and to score a small system that is honestly evaluated above an ambitious one that is not.

modules.title: Scope, and commit to it in writing

items.title: Three candidates, and the criteria that choose between them
checkpoints: Selection criteria written before the candidates
Three genuinely different systems described
Each scored against the criteria
The winner chosen and the runner-up's strongest argument recorded
items.brief: Write the criteria for choosing a capstone before you write the candidates: who it is for, what evidence it can produce, what it would cost to run, and whether it can be evaluated at all. Then describe three genuinely different systems and score each. Record the runner-up's strongest argument, because in four weeks you will wonder whether you picked wrong and the honest answer should already be written down.

items.title: Does this need AI at all
checkpoints: The core task isolated
A non-AI approach specified in enough detail to cost
Both approaches costed at a stated volume
The decision recorded with the conditions that would reverse it
items.brief: Apply AIE-107 to your own capstone before building it. Isolate the core task and specify a non-AI approach in enough detail that you could cost it — rules, a lookup, a classical model, or a human doing it. Cost both at a realistic volume. If the honest answer is that the system does not need a model, change the capstone rather than the answer; a capstone chosen because it needs AI is a better capstone than one that merely tolerates it.

items.title: The evaluation plan, registered before any code
checkpoints: The success criterion stated as a number with a threshold
The eval method specified, including negatives
A baseline named that the system must beat
Committed to a timestamped record before implementation begins
items.brief: Write and register the evaluation before writing any code: what number defines success, what threshold you will accept, what the negatives look like, and which baseline the system must beat. Commit it with a timestamp. Every course in this programme has argued that the measurement must predate the thing measured, and this is the item where you do it for work of your own choosing.

items.title: What you will not build
checkpoints: At least six excluded features listed
Each with the reason for exclusion
The 120-hour budget allocated across the remaining modules
A named trigger for cutting further
items.brief: List at least six things a reasonable person would expect this system to do, and exclude them. Give the reason for each. Then allocate the remaining 120 hours across the phases below and name the trigger that will make you cut further — a date, or an hours-spent threshold. Capstones fail by scope, not by difficulty, and a scope you have not written down is one you will quietly expand.

items.title: Data handling and risk, before there is data
checkpoints: Every category of data the system will touch listed
Retention and deletion decided per category
The failure that would most embarrass you identified
A mitigation or an accepted-risk statement for each
items.brief: List every category of data this system will touch, including logs and traces. Decide retention and deletion for each before the first row exists, because retrofitting deletion is how personal data ends up living forever in a backup. Then name the failure that would most embarrass you in public and either mitigate it or write down that you are accepting the risk and why.

items.title: Publish the scope document
checkpoints: Scope, exclusions, evaluation plan and baseline in one public document
What already existed before the capstone stated explicitly
Published before implementation begins
Linked from the public log
items.brief: Publish the scope document publicly before you write code. It carries the selection, the exclusions, the registered evaluation and the baseline, and it states plainly what existed before this capstone started so the boundary of new work is checkable by a reader. Publishing it in advance is what makes every later claim about intent verifiable rather than reconstructed.

items.title: Retention: the registered scope and its thresholds
The walking skeleton
checkpoints: End-to-end path working with the simplest possible behaviour
Deployed somewhere reachable from the internet
One real request served and logged
Committed and reproducible from a clean checkout
items.brief: Build the thinnest possible end-to-end path and deploy it: request in, trivial answer out, logged. No intelligence yet. Doing this first means every later component lands in a system that already exists rather than accumulating toward one, and it moves the deployment problem to the day when nothing is at stake.

items.title: The core capability, first pass
checkpoints: The main task working on a handful of real inputs
Prompt or model choice recorded with its reason
Known failure cases collected as they appear
No evaluation yet — that is M3
items.brief: Make the system do its actual job, badly, on real inputs. Record why you chose the model and the approach. Start a file of failure cases the moment you see the first one — these become the regression corpus later, and the ones you notice now are the ones you will have forgotten by then.

items.title: Context and retrieval, or the argument for not having it
checkpoints: A context strategy chosen and implemented, or explicitly declined
The choice justified against the corpus's actual properties
Context budget stated in tokens
Retrieval evaluated separately from generation, if present
items.brief: Decide what the model needs to see and implement it — retrieval, a fixed context, or nothing. Justify the choice against the properties of your actual corpus, as AIE-103 argued: dense proper nouns favour lexical search, near-synonymous prose favours embeddings. If you decline retrieval entirely, that is a legitimate answer and it needs the same justification. State the context budget in tokens, because you now know what those cost.

items.title: Output that cannot be malformed
checkpoints: A schema defined for every model output the system depends on
Validation at the boundary, with the invalid payload retained
Behaviour on validation failure defined and tested
A deliberate malformed response injected to prove the path
items.brief: Define a schema for every model output the system relies on and validate at the boundary. When validation fails, retain the invalid payload — a rejected response that is discarded is a bug you cannot investigate. Prove the path works by injecting a malformed response deliberately, because this code runs rarely and is therefore the code most likely to be wrong.

items.title: Failing closed
checkpoints: Every external dependency's failure mode enumerated
Timeouts set explicitly rather than inherited
The degraded behaviour defined and visible to the user
A dependency failure simulated end to end
items.brief: Enumerate what happens when each external dependency fails: the model API, the datastore, the network. Set every timeout explicitly — an inherited default is a decision someone else made about your product. Define what the user sees when the system is degraded, and make it honest rather than a spinner. Then simulate a real failure and confirm the system does what you said.

items.title: Cost and latency instrumented from the start
checkpoints: Per-request token counts and cost recorded
Latency recorded per stage, not only end to end
A cost-per-thousand-requests figure computed
The data written somewhere queryable
items.brief: Record tokens, cost and per-stage latency for every request from the first real one. AIE-105 argued that cost is a design constraint rather than a bill you read later, and instrumenting on day one is the difference between knowing what a change cost and estimating it. Compute a cost per thousand requests now, while the number is small enough to be surprising.

items.title: An interface a stranger can use
checkpoints: The primary task completable without instruction
The system's limits stated in the interface itself
Error states written for someone who does not know the internals
Tested by watching someone use it without help
items.brief: Build the interface to the standard of someone arriving with no context. State the system's limits in the interface rather than in a README nobody opens. Write error messages for a person who does not know your architecture. Then watch one real person use it without helping them, and write down every point at which you wanted to intervene.

items.title: Deploy it properly
checkpoints: Reproducible deployment from a clean checkout
Secrets outside the repository and outside the tree
State outside the deployable artifact
A rollback path tested, not assumed
items.brief: Make the deployment reproducible and boring. Secrets outside the repo, state outside the artifact, and a rollback you have actually performed rather than one you believe exists. This programme runs on a box where a failed build once overwrote a running server's assets and the service reported healthy while serving nothing — deployment failures are quiet, and the only defence is having tested the recovery.

items.title: Observability, so failures are visible
checkpoints: Full traces retained for a stated window
A way to find the requests that went wrong without reading everything
An alert or check that would catch total failure
Retention consistent with the M1.5 data decisions
items.brief: Make it possible to answer 'what went wrong for that user' without reading every log line. Retain full traces for a window you state, consistent with the data decisions you already registered. Add one check that would catch the system being entirely broken, because the failure that costs most is the one nobody notices for a week.

items.title: The first external user
checkpoints: At least one person who is not you uses it unaided
Their session observed or recorded with consent
Every point of confusion logged
One change made in response, and its effect checked
items.brief: Put the system in front of at least one person who is not you and does not work on it, with their consent to observe. Do not help them. Log every point of confusion and every assumption they made that you did not expect. Make one change in response and check whether it helped. This is the item that separates a capstone from a demo, and it is routinely skipped because it is uncomfortable.

items.title: Retention: the system's architecture and failure paths

modules.title: Evaluate, against the plan you registered

items.title: Build the eval set the plan specified
checkpoints: Cases built to the registered specification
Negatives included at the stated proportion
Every case carrying its provenance
Loaded and validated by the harness
items.brief: Build the evaluation set your M1.3 plan specified, at the size it specified, with the negatives it specified. Record where each case came from. Load it into tools/eval-harness so the format is validated rather than trusted — the harness rejects a corpus with untagged cases or spans that are not verbatim in their source, and those are exactly the errors that make a gold set quietly wrong.

items.title: Run it, and record the baseline
checkpoints: The system scored through the harness
Per-tag results reported, not only the aggregate
A baseline frozen for future comparison
The result compared against the registered threshold
items.brief: Score the system through the harness and read the per-tag results rather than the headline number. Freeze the run as a baseline. Then compare against the threshold you registered in M1.3 and state plainly whether you hit it. This is the moment the registered plan pays for itself, and it is the moment most projects renegotiate their success criterion instead.

items.title: Error analysis on real traces
checkpoints: At least 50 real traces read individually
Failures open-coded rather than bucketed in advance
Categories counted and ranked
The top category traced to a specific cause
items.brief: Read at least fifty real traces one at a time and code the failures as you find them rather than sorting them into categories you decided in advance. Count and rank the categories. Then take the largest and find its actual cause in the system. AIE-102 argued that error analysis beats eval design as a first move; this is where you do it on a system you built to your own specification.

items.title: Beat the baseline you named
checkpoints: The M1.3 baseline implemented properly, not as a straw man
Both evaluated on the identical set through the same harness
The comparison stated with an interval
A verdict recorded even where it is unflattering
items.brief: Implement the baseline you named in the registered plan, and implement it in good faith. Evaluate both on the identical set. State the comparison with an interval rather than two numbers. If the baseline wins, that is the finding, it goes in the write-up, and it is worth more to a reader than a system that beat nothing.

items.title: How much of this is noise
checkpoints: The eval re-run several times with sampling enabled
Run-to-run variation quantified
An interval computed for the headline number
The smallest detectable difference stated
items.brief: Run the same evaluation several times without changing anything and measure how much the number moves. Compute an interval. Then state the smallest difference this eval could detect — that figure governs every improvement claim you will make for the rest of the project, and knowing it stops you reporting a two-point gain that your own harness cannot distinguish from nothing.

items.title: A regression suite that runs itself
checkpoints: Every failure case from M2.2 onward turned into a case
The suite wired to run automatically
Non-zero exit on regression against the frozen baseline
One deliberate regression introduced to prove it fires
items.brief: Turn the failure file you have been keeping since M2.2 into a regression suite, wire it to run automatically, and make it fail the build on regression against the frozen baseline. Then break something on purpose and confirm it fires. A check that has never been seen to fail is a check nobody should trust, and this programme has already caught two of those in its own tooling.

items.title: Act on the error analysis, and measure
checkpoints: One change made addressing the top failure category
Expected effect predicted before the change
Re-evaluated on the identical set
Result compared against both the prediction and the noise floor
items.brief: Make one change targeting the largest failure category, and predict its effect before making it. Re-evaluate. Compare the outcome against your prediction and against the smallest detectable difference from M3.5. A gain smaller than your noise floor is not a gain, and reporting it as one is the most common dishonesty in applied machine learning.

items.title: Where this system stops working
checkpoints: The failure boundary probed deliberately
The conditions under which quality collapses identified
The boundary quantified rather than described
Recorded as the capability's negative result
items.brief: Find where your system stops working and write it down with numbers: input length, domain distance, language, ambiguity, volume. Every capability claim in this programme requires a documented negative result, and this is the item that produces one for the capstone. Anyone can ship a demo; the boundary is the part a reader learns from.

items.title: Retention: the system's measured behaviour and limits
Red-team your own system
checkpoints: An attack surface enumerated for this specific system
Prompt injection attempted through every input path
Successful attacks recorded verbatim
Mitigations applied and re-tested
items.brief: Attack your own system deliberately. Enumerate every path by which text you did not write reaches the model — user input, retrieved documents, tool results, file names. Attempt injection through each. Record what worked, exactly. Apply mitigations and try again. The attacks that still work after mitigation go in the write-up, because a security section listing only solved problems tells a reader nothing.

items.title: The controls that actually hold
checkpoints: Authentication and authorisation implemented if there is anything to protect
Rate limiting in place with a stated threshold
Input size bounded
Each control tested by attempting to violate it
items.brief: Implement the controls the system actually needs — access control if there is anything to protect, rate limiting with a threshold you chose rather than inherited, bounded input sizes. Test each by attempting to violate it. An unbounded input field in front of a per-token bill is a funding request from a stranger.

items.title: What it costs under load
checkpoints: A load profile defined and justified
The system run under it
Cost and latency at load compared against the single-request figures
The breaking point identified
items.brief: Define a realistic load, run the system under it, and compare cost and latency against your single-request numbers from M2.6. They will not scale linearly. Find the point at which the system stops meeting its latency target or its cost stops being acceptable, and state it as a number of concurrent users. A system whose breaking point is unknown is one you cannot responsibly show anyone.

items.title: The failure drill
checkpoints: The model provider's failure simulated
The datastore's failure simulated
A bad deploy performed and rolled back
Time to detect and time to recover recorded for each
items.brief: Break the system on purpose in three ways and recover from each: the model provider unavailable, the datastore unavailable, and a bad deploy. Record how long detection took and how long recovery took. The numbers matter less than discovering which failure you had no plan for, which is always one of them.

items.title: What you would not ship to a paying customer
checkpoints: An honest list of what is not production-grade
Each item's risk stated concretely
The work required to close each estimated
A judgement on which would be worth doing
items.brief: Write the list you would give a colleague inheriting this system: what is not production-grade, what risk each thing carries, and roughly what it would cost to fix. Then say which you would actually do and which you would accept. This list is the single most credible thing in a capstone write-up, because everyone who has shipped anything knows it exists and most authors pretend theirs does not.

items.title: The runbook someone else could operate from
checkpoints: Every routine operation documented as steps, not prose
Each failure from the M4.4 drill given a procedure
Where the secrets, the data and the logs live, stated
Tested by following it exactly, without improvising
items.brief: Write the document that lets someone who is not you keep this running: how to deploy, how to roll back, where the secrets and the data and the logs live, and what to do for each failure you drilled in M4.4. Then test it the only way that works — follow it exactly, without using anything you know that is not written down. Every step you had to improvise is a step that was missing, and finding them now is cheaper than finding them during an outage.

items.title: Retention: attack surface and operational limits

modules.title: Write it up, and ship it

items.title: The ten-minute assessment
checkpoints: What it does, for whom, in the first paragraph
The headline number with its interval, above the fold
The limitations visible without scrolling past praise
A working link a reader can use immediately
items.brief: Write the document a hiring manager reads in ten minutes and then decides. What it does and for whom in the first paragraph; the headline number with its interval near the top; the limitations where they cannot be missed; a link that works. Most capstone write-ups bury the result under a narrative of the journey. Yours puts the result first and the journey underneath, where the reader can choose it.

items.title: The technical write-up
checkpoints: Every significant decision recorded with its alternative
Each marked as measured or inherited
The evaluation method described well enough to criticise
The error analysis and its consequences included
items.brief: Write the version for someone who wants to argue with you. Every significant decision, its alternative, and whether it was measured or inherited — the distinction AIE-204 introduced, and the one almost no published write-up makes. Describe the evaluation in enough detail that a reader could attack it, because an evaluation nobody can criticise is one nobody can trust.

items.title: The chapter that connects backwards
checkpoints: Published into the public engineering log
Connected to at least three earlier chapters
At least one earlier conclusion revised
Stands alone on its own page
items.brief: Publish the capstone chapter into the growing public log. It must stand alone and must connect to at least three earlier chapters — and it must revise at least one earlier conclusion, because after twelve courses and a shipped system, something you wrote in the first six weeks is now wrong. Finding it and correcting it in public is the point of keeping one log rather than six posts.

items.title: The limitations section, written honestly
checkpoints: The negative result from M3.8 stated prominently
Every unfavourable measurement included
The gap between registered scope and delivered system stated
Nothing removed between draft and publication
items.brief: Write the limitations from the measurements rather than from modesty. The failure boundary from M3.8, every unfavourable number, and the honest gap between what M1.6 registered and what you actually delivered. Then check your draft against your published scope document and confirm nothing quietly disappeared between them.

items.title: Ship it publicly
checkpoints: Live at a public URL a stranger can reach
Source public, or the reason for keeping it closed stated
Running cost stated and sustainable
A stated intention for how long it will stay up
items.brief: Put it in the world. A public URL that works without you, source public unless you can state why not, and a running cost you can sustain. Say how long you intend to keep it up — a capstone that quietly disappears in three months makes every link in the transcript dead, and stating a horizon in advance is more honest than letting it rot.

items.title: Update the capability claims this earns
checkpoints: Each capability this system evidences identified
The specific evidence named per claim
Claims the system does not support explicitly declined
The artifact and negative-result fields updated where earned
items.brief: Go through the capability pages and decide what this system actually earns. For each claim you make, name the specific evidence. For each one it does not support, say so and leave it unearned. The temptation at the end of a capstone is to let one system justify every line on the CV, and refusing that is the whole reason the evidence ledger exists.

items.title: Retention: the write-up's claims and their evidence
The questions you are afraid of
checkpoints: At least fifteen questions written, targeting real weaknesses
Answers drafted for each
The three with no good answer identified
Those three addressed in the write-up rather than hidden
items.brief: Write the fifteen questions you least want to be asked about this system, aimed at real weaknesses rather than easy ones. Draft answers. Identify the three you cannot answer well, and put those into the write-up as acknowledged limitations rather than hoping nobody asks. A question you have already conceded in writing cannot be used against you.

items.title: The capstone defense
checkpoints: Questions generated at defense time from the published artifacts
Answered aloud without notes and without the system open
At least one hostile line of questioning pursued to its end
Recording retained
items.brief: The longest defense in the programme, because it covers a whole system rather than one assignment. Questions are generated at defense time from your published write-up and repository. Answered aloud, without notes and without the system open in front of you. At least one line of questioning is pursued past the point of comfort, because the difference between a system you built and one you assembled shows up three questions deep, not one.

items.title: Correct what the defense exposed
checkpoints: Every point where the defense revealed an error listed
The write-up corrected rather than annotated
The correction dated and visible
Anything that turned out to be unfixable stated as such
items.brief: The defense will expose errors — a number you could not justify, a decision you could not reconstruct, a claim broader than the evidence. Correct the published write-up rather than leaving it and adding a note. Date the correction and leave it visible. A public document that quietly changes is worse than one that was wrong, and a visible correction is the strongest possible evidence that the rest is honest.

items.title: What you would do differently
checkpoints: The largest wrong decision identified
The point at which it could have been caught named
What would have caught it stated as a practice, not a resolution
One practice actually adopted
items.brief: Name the largest thing you got wrong, and the moment at which it was still cheap to catch. Then convert that into a practice rather than a resolution — 'register the evaluation before building' is a practice, 'be more careful' is not. Adopt one of them formally, by writing it into the rules of a repository you own, so the lesson survives your memory of this project.

three candidates scored against every criterion

levels.3: Materially different in the evidence they could produce, not just in subject.

criteria.criterion: The comparison uses real numbers

levels.3: Both costed at a stated volume with accuracy, latency and maintenance included.

a named baseline the system must beat
committed with a verifiable timestamp

a cut trigger stated as a date or an hours threshold

logs and traces included as categories

criteria.criterion: Accepted risks are stated as accepted

reproducible from a clean checkout

a failure-case file started and non-empty

retrieval evaluated separately from generation where present

criteria.criterion: The strategy fits the corpus's actual properties

levels.3: Justified against measured properties of the corpus.

levels.3: Argued with what would change the decision.

a malformed response injected and the path exercised

criteria.criterion: Behaviour on failure is a decision

a dependency failure simulated end to end

criteria.criterion: Timeouts are chosen rather than inherited

cost per thousand requests computed

limits stated in the interface itself

levels.3: Plain language stating what to do next.

criteria.criterion: The observation was not interfered with

a rollback actually performed, not merely available

criteria.criterion: The rollback is proven

levels.3: Performed, with time-to-recover recorded.

criteria.criterion: The deploy is reproducible by someone else

levels.0: Manual steps in the author's head.
levels.3: Scripted, with a failure in the script causing the deploy to stop rather than continue.

a check that would catch total failure

criteria.criterion: A specific bad request can be found

levels.3: Traces retrievable with the full input and output of each stage.

criteria.criterion: Retention matches the registered decision

levels.3: Matches, with deletion demonstrated.

criteria.criterion: The failure check is meaningful

levels.3: A functional check that would have caught a past real failure mode.

one change made in response and its effect checked

criteria.criterion: The session was genuinely unaided

levels.3: Unaided, with the author's own interventions they resisted noted.

criteria.criterion: Confusion is recorded specifically

completion.required: All thirty-eight assignments and projects and the defense submitted. This course has no tier-0 items: there is nothing to read here, only work to do.
completion.grade_rollup: Deterministic. Each item's tier sets its weight; panel scores enter as per-criterion values; nothing is rounded up. Computed in TypeScript, never by a model.
completion.mastery_note: Sets initial mastery on evaluation design, approach selection and deployment, and is the only course whose output is intended to be opened by a stranger. Its defense is the longest in the programme because it covers a whole system rather than a single assignment.
